features: Fixed — REOPENING A SUPPLIER PAYMENT FOR EDITING MULTIPLIED THE BANK FEES BY ONE HUNDRED. A payment carrying €2.50 of bank fees, reopened for editing to correct a date or a reference, showed €25,000.00 in the fees box. Saving without even touching that field wrote €25,000.00 to the database: the original figure multiplied by ten thousand. Money travels through the system as whole cents — €2.50 is 250 — and the edit screen, instead of dividing by one hundred to bring the figure back to euros, multiplied it a second time.

No database changes in this version: no migrations and no data repaired retroactively. Anyone who finds an inflated fee on a payment that was edited can correct it by reopening that payment for editing: the box now shows the right figure, and saving again is enough.

The defect struck even without touching the field: opening the payment for editing and saving was enough. The other amounts on the same screen — gross, withholding and net — were handled correctly: the fees alone carried one conversion too many, inside the very same object.
Recording a new payment was never affected: there the fees box starts at zero and the conversion to cents happens once, at the right moment.

Why no check had caught it: the inflated figure entered double-entry on both sides — debiting «bank charges» and crediting the bank — so the accounting entry balanced perfectly and the balance validator had nothing to report. The only possible signal was the bank account balance dropping by €25,000 instead of €2.50, or an «insufficient funds» block on a payment whose amount had not been changed.

The client-side money module knew how to turn typed euros into cents, but not the other way round: the inverse conversion — the one needed whenever an edit form is prefilled with an already saved amount — did not exist, and whoever had needed it had written it by hand, backwards. The two conversions now sit side by side, spelling out which is the entry boundary and which the exit one.

The defect is pinned from both sides. A JavaScript test actually mounts the edit screen and checks the number that ends up in the box, because the error lived in the form's initialisation and a test on the logic alone would never have reached it. A PHP test pins the server's reference: that the screen receives whole cents, and that opening and re-saving twice in a row leaves the figure where it was.
